# A word about Glenmore

I have some news about the house in Glenmore, and I should have put it here before now. Úna set up this blog years ago so that the cousins in Boston and Perth and Leeds could keep up with us, and it is the right place to tell everyone the same thing, in my own words.

I have agreed a sale on the house. The sale was agreed on 3 November, and it is due to close on **15 January 2027**. I want that date written down plainly, so that nobody has to hear it from somebody else or wonder whether what they have heard is right.

Some of you already knew. Some heard it second-hand, before I had told you properly, and I am sorry for that. It was my responsibility to tell you. I put it off because I knew it would be difficult, and putting it off made it more difficult and more hurtful than it needed to be.

I am not writing to ask everyone to be pleased about the sale. I know that some of you will be sad, and some will disagree with me. But I would rather you heard the reasons from me than have them travelling round in bits on the phone, with everyone trying to work out what has happened and why.

The house near Oughterard was built in 1931 by Tom’s grandfather, Pádraig Mulkerrin. It was the old Mulkerrin place long before I had anything to do with it. Tom grew up there. For some of you, it has been there for your whole lives, something you could picture without having to think about it, whether you were down the road or on the other side of the world.

I know I am selling a house that belongs in other people’s memories as well as my own. That is part of what made telling you so hard. It is not an excuse for failing to do it.

Since Tom died in March 2024, I have been driving out every fortnight to air the house and check the pipes. It is forty minutes each way. That may not sound much, and on a fine day the drive itself is no hardship. But there is always the journey back, and another visit due, and the question of what I will find when I open the door.

For a while, going out gave me something definite to do. There was a practical job in front of me, and I could get on with it. Open up, let the air through, check that everything was all right. I knew how to do those things even when I did not know quite what to do with myself.

But it has not become easier with time. I cannot go on maintaining it, and I need to say that without following it immediately with an assurance that I will manage somehow. I have been saying that to myself for long enough.

There is something else I have not told any of you. Last February, I slipped on the step at the back door in the frost. I was alone. I lay there for twenty minutes before I could get up.

I told nobody at the time. I did not want the fuss, and once I was up I persuaded myself there was nothing to tell. That was foolish. I would have had plenty to say to anyone else who kept such a thing to themselves.

The truth is that I have been afraid of being alone at the house since then. I still go, but I am afraid. I think about that step, and about how long I might be there if it happened again and I could not get up. I am seventy-one. I do not say that as though I am ready to be wrapped in a blanket and put away, but I cannot ignore it either.

I am telling you about the fall because you should know, and because it is one of the reasons for the decision. I am not telling you so that nobody can argue with me. You are allowed to have your own feelings about the house. I need you to understand what looking after it has become for me.

There are the repairs as well. Ó Flaithearta’s surveyed the roof in September. The slates and the back chimney need work, and the quote was €38,000. There is damp in the back bedroom on top of that. The septic tank needs replacing if the house is to be sold to anyone anyway.

These are not small jobs that I have mistaken for a catastrophe. Nor are they things I can keep putting off because the house has stood since 1931 and will surely stand another winter. They need attention, money and somebody to take responsibility for getting them done.

I do not want to spend the coming years worrying about the next repair, or driving out because I am afraid of what might happen if I do not. I know there may be people reading this who would have offered to help if I had asked. I should have talked more openly about how things were. But I have come to the point where I do not want to carry on with the house, even with help.

That is a hard thing to write. It is also the truth.

The buyers are a young couple, Aoife and Kevin Joyce. Kevin is from Maam Cross, and they have two small children. They want to live in the house. It is not being bought as a holiday let.

That mattered to me. The price was fair, but it was less than the Dublin crowd offered in the summer. I took the lower offer on purpose. I do not expect a medal for that, and I am not suggesting that money does not matter. It does. But I was able to take account of who would be living there, and I did.

I wanted the house to be somebody’s home again. That does not make handing it over easy, but it makes a difference to me to know that the Joyces intend to make their life there with their children.

Tom always said the house should have children in it, not be a museum. I have thought about that often. I am not going to claim that I know exactly what he would say about every part of this, or use his words to settle an argument he is not here to join. But he did say it, and those of you who heard him will remember.

When I think of the children there, I think of the lake below the house and them learning to swim. I think particularly of Declan refusing to come out until his lips were blue. There was no convincing him he was cold. Apparently the rest of us could see it, but he knew better.

I cannot look at that lake without remembering them as they were then. I do not imagine that will change because somebody else has the keys to the house.

And before any of that, there was Tom asking me to marry him in the haggard behind the house in 1979. It was raining, and the cattle were watching. Of all the places he might have chosen, that was where he did it. I said yes, as you know.

I have been thinking about that day while dealing with surveys and quotes and the business of selling. It is a peculiar thing to have a house described in terms of its roof and its septic tank when you can stand behind it and remember being asked to marry the man you loved. Both things are true, however little they seem to have to do with each other.

That is why I do understand the upset. I am not looking at the place and seeing only work to be done. I see Tom there too. I see the children, and all the years between that wet day in 1979 and now.

Over the best part of two years, I have come to realise that I can keep Tom’s memory without keeping the house. I did not believe that simply because it was a sensible thing somebody might say. It has taken me this long to feel that it is true for me.

I still miss him. Selling the house will not bring that to an end, any more than keeping it would bring him back. I can know that perfectly well and still find myself standing in a room, reluctant to leave it. There is nothing very tidy about any of this.

I also want to say something about Declan, because he was badly hurt by how he found out, and I was responsible for that.

He heard from his cousin Gráinne in a WhatsApp message, not from me. He rang me at two in the morning his time. He said I was “selling Dad”. I said things back that I should not have said.

I am not going to put the whole of that conversation here. It was painful enough between the two of us. But I will not give everyone a pleasant account of the sale and leave out the fact that I hurt my son, first by not telling him and then in what I said when he rang.

Declan, I should have spoken to you before agreeing the sale. I regret not consulting you. You should not have had to learn about it from Gráinne, and she should not have been put in the position of being the person who told you. I am sorry for that, and for the things I said on the phone.

I am not angry with you. I know you love your dad, and I know what the house means to you. You do not have to pretend that you are all right with this for us to speak again.

But I am not willing to wait until your summer visit. The sale is due to close on 15 January, and I intend to go ahead. I know that will be difficult to read. I do not want to soften it into something that leaves you thinking the decision is still waiting to be made.

I can be sorry for the way I handled it and still believe that selling is the right thing for me to do. Those are not comfortable things to hold together, but that is where I am.

The door is open, Declan. Ring me. We do not have to finish the whole argument in one conversation, and we do not have to agree before we can talk. I would very much like to hear from you.

For everyone asking what will happen to the things in the house, there are some I want you to know are being kept.

The dresser is going to Úna’s. Pádraig’s fiddle is staying with the family, and so are the photographs, the Sacred Heart lamp and the gate sign. They are not going with the sale.

I know the dresser will be one of the first things some of you wonder about. I am glad we know where it is going. And I want the photographs kept, including the ones that need somebody to tell us who is in them. If you are looking through them with us, please say what you know. I would rather hear a name or a story twice than discover later that nobody thought to ask.

Keeping these things does not mean I think the rest of the house can be packed up and carried away in pieces. It cannot. There will be things we miss that are not ours to take. But I wanted you to know what is being kept, rather than worry that everything is being cleared out without a thought.

Aoife and Kevin have also said that family can come out and walk the land any time. I was very grateful for that. It is a kindness, and I hope we will treat it as one, remembering that the place will be their home. It does not mean everything will stay as it was, but it means we need not think of the land as somewhere we can never set foot again.

Before the house is cleared, I would like us to have a day there together.

**Please come on Sunday, 13 December, if you can.** We will have soup and sandwiches. Bring wellies.

There is no need to arrive with a speech, or to know what you think about the sale. You can be sad about it and still come. You can disagree with me and still have a sandwich. I would like to see you.

We can walk, look through the photographs, and spend a bit of time in the house without making the whole day about what needs doing next. If there is a memory you want to share, I would love to hear it. If you would rather have a quiet look around, that is all right too.

I know December is not easy, especially for those of you in Boston and Perth and Leeds, and that most people cannot simply arrange a journey because I have put a date on the blog. Please do not feel that being unable to come says anything about how much the place matters to you. I know better than that.

But anyone who can come is welcome. Let me know if you think you will make it, so we have enough soup, though I would rather have an unexpected person at the door than have somebody stay away because they had not given notice.

I wish I had told you all sooner. I wish I had spoken to Declan before there was anything for Gráinne to pass on. Those are things I could have done differently, and should have.

The decision itself is one I have reached slowly. I am tired of the responsibility, I am afraid on my own there, and I cannot go on maintaining the house. I also want to be able to remember it with pleasure, without every thought of it leading to something I must check or fix or pay for.

So, to make sure the news is clear: the sale to Aoife and Kevin Joyce is agreed, and it is due to close on **15 January 2027**. The family day is **Sunday, 13 December**, before the house is cleared.

I will be sad to hand over the keys. I expect I will be relieved as well. I am glad there will be children living there again.

I hope to see as many of you as possible in December. Wear something warm, bring the wellies, and come in for a bowl of soup.
